For most of the year, Pema, twenty-six, had felt flat: work, sleep, the same videos. In April she signed up for the Tuesday pottery class at the community centre in Gangtok, mostly because the poster had a messy handprint on it. Varun, the instructor, handed her a lump of clay. "It'll collapse the first ten times. That's the class." It collapsed. She laughed out loud for the first time in weeks. By June she was helping the older ladies centre their clay and staying to sweep up.
But some weeks the heaviness still came back and sat on her for days. So one Tuesday, before class, she stopped at the centre's health desk and booked a session with the visiting counsellor. Pottery helped. She just didn't want to wait and see if it was enough.

Dear Jhanvi,
You asked why I sound more like myself lately. Here's the honest answer.
For about eight months, everything felt flat. Not tragic, just grey. Office, metro, dinner, phone, sleep. I stopped wanting anything.
So I changed one pattern. I started cycling to work twice a week instead of taking the metro. Then I signed up to coach chess on Sunday mornings at the children's library near my flat. Twelve kids, total chaos, one boy who cries every time he loses a knight. I actually look forward to it.
The other thing, and I'm telling you because you're my sister: the flatness was getting heavy, so I went to a doctor, and she referred me to a counsellor. Three sessions so far. I'm not fixed, but I'm not waiting it out alone any more.
Love,
Nitin

My job was fine. My life was fine. Everything was fine and flat. I'd come home and lie on the sofa until midnight.
First I tried something small. I joined a Saturday pottery class. I was terrible. The first bowl collapsed. I laughed for the first time in weeks.
Then I signed up to teach English to kids at the community centre on Sundays. Those kids didn't care that I was tired. They wanted me there.
But some weeks the heaviness was still sitting on my chest, week after week. So I talked to a counsellor. That helped me see the flatness wasn't laziness, and what to do about it.
Pottery, kids, a counsellor. That's how.

I'm Hemant, and I've shared a flat with Tanvir for two years, so I saw most of it.
Last winter he came home, dropped his bag and lay on the sofa with his phone until one or two. Every night. He wasn't miserable, he said. Just bored of everything.
Then in February I noticed a toolbox by the door. He'd signed up for a cycle-repair course at the community workshop. Saturdays, he came back with oily hands, talking fast about gears.
In March he started helping at the food bank on Tuesday evenings. He didn't say much about it, but he started cooking dinner again.
One night he told me the grey feeling still came back some weeks, heavy. He'd booked an appointment with a doctor to talk about it. I thought that was braver than any of the rest.
I don't know what's in his head. But he laughs more now.

Next step: I'll check in with her at the end of the month.

Sister Agnes, hostel mentor
